prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots place B033 first, and I do not treat that agreement as merit in itself. On the evidence, GLP-1 is a rare unbroken chain from hormone physiology (incretin effect, proglucagon processing, the active truncated peptide, receptor biology and actions on islets, appetite and gastric emptying) to approved drugs with large randomized outcome trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. It is original, mature, independently confirmed and still expanding. A three-person prize built on the physiology (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) rewards discovery in the sense the prize has traditionally favoured, while the citation leaves room to acknowledge the therapies that followed.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely contested. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against Habener and colleagues cannot be resolved from the supplied text, and Habener is outside the credited names. The three-person cap also excludes Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose medicinal chemistry produced liraglutide and semaglutide, the drugs that delivered the patient impact. If the committee thinks the impact lies mainly in the drugs, a physiology-only prize looks incomplete. If it thinks the discovery lies in the physiology, the priority question around Mojsov weakens the claim that this trio is the correct one.

responses.point: Perlmann favours the three basic-science contributors but says Knudsen's industrial drug development could alternatively fill the third slot, and he ranks nusinersen (B045) third.
responses.response: I agree on the three basic contributors but would not give the third slot to Knudsen. Her work is excellent pharmaceutical development, but the Prize is better placed recognizing the identification of the active peptide and its physiology. Replacing Mojsov with Knudsen would turn the prize into a drug-development award and leave the discovery of the active form unrewarded. I accept that the Mojsov priority dispute is a real weakness, and I would want it examined in round 2 rather than assumed away. On B045 I rank it below UPR and optogenetics because the SMN2 splicing mechanism is elegant, but the contribution is tied to one drug and the SMN gene discoverers sit outside the credited names.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks BCR-ABL inhibition and imatinib (B032) second, as a paradigm of targeted therapy that is fully confirmed and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept that B032 is mature and clinically decisive, and I did not rank it in my opening eight, which I should defend. My reservation is that Lydon, Druker and Sawyers are mostly credited for drug development, resistance biology and clinical proof, while the underlying oncogene work lies outside the credited set and was recognized earlier within the kinase and oncogene field. That makes it more an application than a discovery. I would put it below B026 and B033, though I do not think it is a weak candidate and I would not oppose it as an alternative if the committee wants a targeted-therapy prize.

responses.point: El-Manira places CAR-T (B026) second but includes only June and Sadelain, because Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy claim leaves the third slot unsettled. He also lists the 3-person optogenetics trio third and notes the six-name problem.
responses.response: I share his June and Sadelain pairing for CAR-T and agree Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work is a separate line that should not be folded into the core CAR invention, unlike the three-name set recorded in the shortlist. Where I differ is on optogenetics. He ranks it third on discovery impact, and I weigh the method as impressive but with six credible contributors, a trio inevitably leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, and I doubt the committee can defend that cut. For that reason I keep it behind CAR-T and the UPR as a fallback rather than a lead candidate.

responses.point: The chair argues the physiology trio is the most defensible, with Mojsov's priority against other groups for the active truncated form unresolved by the supplied text, and that Knudsen's role is major but industrial.
responses.response: I agree with this framing and with the chair's point that Habener's absence from the credited list limits how fair any configuration can be. I would go one step further: the committee should treat the Mojsov question as an open uncertainty to be checked against the record before a final ballot, not as grounds to drop her. I also note his ranking of B048 sixth and the HPV vaccine fifth. I see the UPR as the stronger fundamental discovery, because the HPV vaccine overlaps with the 2008 prize and has shared priority among several VLP groups.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (B051) second as a clean two-person bench-to-bedside story with very broad clinical effect, and sees the recognition as mature rather than premature.
responses.response: The Feldmann and Maini pairing is coherent and the clinical effect is not in question, and I ranked B051 eighth for that reason. My doubt is that the molecular biology of TNF (Cerami, Vilcek, Kollias and others) falls outside the credited names, so the prize would reward the clinical proof of concept and leave out the biology it depends on. Since IL-6 blockade (B008) is on her ballot as well, a prize in this area would invite a harder comparison of cytokine-targeting claims than the supplied ballots resolve.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide, relative to Habener and colleagues, supports her inclusion; the supplied text does not resolve it.
Whether the committee wants to reward GLP-1 physiology or the drug development (Knudsen), since the three-person cap forces a choice.
Whether Rosenberg belongs with June and Sadelain on B026, and how to treat Eshhar and other early CAR originators outside the credited names.
I rely on my own recall of the priority histories for several candidates and have not verified them against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén, and joint work with Christopher Burge's group at MIT. None of these people is credited on a shortlisted ballot, and I have no documented involvement with any shortlisted candidate. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile. Shared KI affiliation with colleagues is not treated as a conflict.
